opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few ingredients that really matter, and honestly, none of them is magic on its own. It's more about getting all of them right at the same time.

The first one is the simulator itself. You need physics that's fast enough to generate huge amounts of experience, because these reinforcement learning policies need millions or even billions of samples. That's why massively parallel simulation on GPUs was such a big deal for us: you can train thousands of robots at once and get a walking policy in minutes instead of days. But speed alone isn't enough. The simulation has to capture the parts of the physics that actually matter for the task.

And that leads to the second point, which is modeling the robot correctly, especially the actuators. A lot of the sim-to-real gap for legged robots comes from the motors and the drivetrain, not from the rigid body dynamics. The real actuators have delays, friction, bandwidth limits, and they don't behave like ideal torque sources. One approach that worked really well is learning an actuator model from real data, basically a small network that maps commands to the torques you actually get, and putting that into the simulator.

The third ingredient is domain randomization. You accept that your simulator will never be perfect, so you randomize the things you're unsure about: masses, friction coefficients, motor strength, latencies, sensor noise, terrain. You also push the robot around with random disturbances. The policy then can't overfit to one particular version of the world, and it has to learn something robust that works across that whole distribution. Hopefully the real world falls somewhere inside it.

Then there's the question of what the policy observes. You have to be careful to only give it information it will actually have on the real robot, with realistic noise. If you use privileged information in simulation, like exact terrain height or contact states, you can do it through a teacher-student setup, where a teacher learns with privileged information and a student learns to imitate it from the realistic sensors only, often using history to infer what it can't see directly.

And finally, I'd say reward design and regularization matter a lot more than people expect. If you only reward the robot for moving forward, it'll find all sorts of weird, jittery, high-frequency behaviors that exploit the simulator. These might look fine in sim but they'll break on hardware or just look terrible. So you add penalties on things like joint accelerations, torques, action rates, foot slipping, and that produces smoother motions that transfer much better.

So, to summarize, it's fast simulation, good actuator modeling, smart randomization, realistic observations, and careful reward shaping. And then a lot of iteration on the real robot, because you always discover something you didn't think of.

r001.rationale: The response explains that actuator modeling must capture how commands become actual torques, including drivetrain effects, delays, friction, and bandwidth limits.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's really the central question in our field, and I'd say it comes down to a few things.

The first is accepting that your simulator is never going to be perfect, and designing around that rather than fighting it. People sometimes think sim-to-real is about making the simulation as accurate as possible, and accuracy helps, but what matters more is that the policy you train is robust to the things the simulator gets wrong. So we do a lot of domain randomization. We randomize the friction of the ground, the mass of the robot, add noise to the observations, apply random pushes to the base. The idea is that the real world should just look like another sample from the distribution the policy has already seen.

The second thing, and this is often underestimated, is the actuators. For legged robots especially, the motors are usually the biggest gap between sim and reality. There are delays, there's backlash, there's a torque-speed relationship that a simple PD controller model in simulation doesn't capture. One approach that worked very well for us was to learn an actuator network from data collected on the real robot, and then put that network into the simulation loop. Suddenly the policy experiences the same kind of response it will see on hardware.

Third, I'd say you need to be careful about what you give the policy as input. If you feed it quantities that are easy to get in simulation but noisy or unavailable on the real robot, like the exact base velocity, you're setting yourself up for failure. You want observations that you can actually measure reliably, and if you need the privileged information, you estimate it, or you use a teacher-student setup where the student only sees what the real robot sees.

And then honestly, the last part is iteration speed. When we moved to massively parallel simulation on GPU, with thousands of robots running at once, training went from days to minutes. That doesn't just make things faster, it changes how you work. You can try a reward tweak, train, deploy on the robot, see it fail, and go back, all in the same afternoon. A lot of what looks like clever design in the final paper was really just many quick iterations of watching the real robot fall over and asking why.

So in short: robustness over fidelity, model the actuators well, be honest about your observations, and iterate fast.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to understand which parts of the simulation need to be accurate and which differences the policy can learn to tolerate. You don’t need a perfect simulation, but you do need to capture the things that really affect the robot’s behavior. For legged robots, that includes the actuator dynamics, delays in the control loop, and the contact between the feet and the ground.

Then, for things you don’t know exactly, you can randomize them during training—friction, mass, or the strength of the motors, for example. The idea is that the real robot becomes one of the variations the policy can handle. But randomization isn’t a substitute for getting the basic model right. If you randomize everything too broadly, you can make learning unnecessarily difficult.

It’s also important that the policy gets observations on the real robot that are consistent with what it saw during training. You can have a very good simulation and still fail because your velocity estimate is noisy or your measurements arrive a little later than expected. So successful transfer is really about the whole system: the simulation, the training setup, the state estimation, and the controller running on the hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to have a simulation that captures the things that really matter for the policy. It doesn’t have to be a perfect model of the world, but things like the actuator dynamics, delays, and contact behavior can make a big difference.

Then you need to account for what you don’t know. We use domain randomization, where we vary parameters like friction, mass, and motor strength during training. The policy has to succeed across those variations, so it can’t rely too much on one particular simulator configuration. We also add noise to the observations and train with disturbances.

But it’s a balance. If you randomize everything over a huge range, you can make the task unnecessarily difficult and end up with a very conservative policy. So you want reasonable models, meaningful randomization, and observations that you can actually obtain on the robot. Then testing on the real system tells you which assumptions you got wrong, and you can improve the simulation from there.
